idiom_name: two-phase initialisation: assign the stored property, then super.init(...) with it
implementation_notes: Swift's initialisation model makes the classic structure unnecessary rather than impossible. Phase 1 assigns an initial value to each stored property, and safety check 1 requires that a designated initializer 'ensure that all of the properties introduced by its class are initialized before it delegates up to a superclass initializer' - only afterwards does it call super.init. The derived object's own stored properties therefore exist, and may be read, before the superclass initializer runs, which is exactly the ordering base-from-member manufactures in C++: compute the payload into a stored property, then pass that property to super.init. Swift has no second base class to move a member into (classes are single-inheritance, structs and enums cannot inherit), and none is needed - the compiler enforces the phase-1 rule that the idiom exists to imitate.
pitfalls: Phase 2 (using self, calling instance methods, writing inherited properties) begins only after super.init returns: reading self before the delegation or assigning an own property after it is a compile error, so the pattern's ordering guarantee is enforced rather than merely conventional.

A convenience initializer must set every property it introduces before delegating across (safety check 4), and a failable initializer that returns nil before super.init must release anything it already set - so the payload cannot be produced lazily by a later phase.

Only classes have superclass initializers: for a struct or enum the 'base' part of the pattern does not exist, and the payload is simply a property - applying the C++ mental model to Swift value types is a category error.
